title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
TipYou don’t need to run this



You don’t have to run this live to follow along. Robert Melendez runs the code on screen, and every output is already on this page. If you want to run it later, the code is in the materials ZIP.
Work in Stata or Python? Every code block has three tabs. The live session and the rendered output are R. The Stata and Python tabs show the same step in your language. Pick a tab once and the whole page follows.

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
0. Setup

RStataPython



library(tidyverse)   # dplyr for the joins, readr for the CSVs
library(readxl)      # the crosswalk is an .xlsx; installs with tidyverse, loads separately
library(here)        # file paths that work wherever this folder sits on your machine
library(janitor)     # tabyl(), for frequency tables you can read



* Run this from the workshop folder (the one holding workshop.Rproj), so the
* relative paths below resolve: File > Change Working Directory, or `cd`.
version 16
clear all
set more off

* One tempfile per table the R version keeps in memory. Stata holds one
* dataset at a time, so each step saves and the next step merges it back.
tempfile mydata socialservices parks ses2010 ses2020 xwalk mydata_zcta10 mydata_nanda


import pandas as pd            # data frames, read_csv / read_stata / merge
from pathlib import Path       # file paths that work wherever this folder sits

# The workshop folder: the one holding workshop.Rproj. Adjust if you moved the script.
ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] if "__file__" in globals() else Path.cwd()
DATA = ROOT / "data"




RStataPython



# Our own data. `zip` is a label: say so, or read_csv guesses "number" and
# 03042 becomes 3042.
mydata <- read_csv(
  here("data", "synthetic_data_v20260924.csv"),
  col_types = cols(zip = col_character())
)

# NaNDA: Social Services, ZCTA 2010, 1990-2022. Same rule for the ZCTA code.
socialservices_zcta10 <- read_csv(
  here("data", "nanda", "nanda_socials_Zcta10_1990-2022_01.csv"),
  col_types = cols(zcta10 = col_character())
)

# Parks and Socioeconomic Status come from ICPSR as .rda files. load() drops an
# object into your session under a name ICPSR picked, and returns that name.
# Print it, then rename it to something you will recognise later.
print(load(here("data", "nanda", "38586-0002-Data.rda")))

[1] "da38586.0002"

# The object keeps Robert's name, parks2022. The file is the 2018 ParkServe
# snapshot (DS0002, 2010 boundaries); ICPSR retitled it in October 2026.
parks2022_zcta10 <- da38586.0002
rm(da38586.0002)

print(load(here("data", "nanda", "38528-0003-Data.rda")))   # SES, ZCTA 2010, 2008-2017

[1] "da38528.0003"

rm(da38528.0008)

* in as 3042. Check what it guessed and pad back to five characters if so.

if _rc tostring zip, replace format(%05.0f)

replace zip = "" if zip == "."
save `mydata'

* NaNDA: Social Services, ZCTA 2010, 1990-2022. Same rule for the ZCTA code.
import delimited using "data/nanda/nanda_socials_Zcta10_1990-2022_01.csv", varnames(1) clear
capture confirm string variable zcta10
if _rc tostring zcta10, replace format(%05.0f)
save `socialservices'

* Parks and Socioeconomic Status: take the Stata format from ICPSR. Variable
* names arrive in upper case, as the ICPSR codebook lists them.
* The object keeps Robert's name, parks2022. The file is the 2018 ParkServe
* snapshot (DS0002, 2010 boundaries); ICPSR retitled it in October 2026.
use "data/nanda/38586-0002-Data.dta", clear          // Parks, ZCTA, 2018
capture confirm string variable ZCTA19
if _rc tostring ZCTA19, replace format(%05.0f)
save `parks'

use "data/nanda/38528-0003-Data.dta", clear          // SES, ZCTA 2010, 2008-2017
capture confirm string variable ZCTA10
if _rc tostring ZCTA10, replace format(%05.0f)
save `ses2010'

use "data/nanda/38528-0008-Data.dta", clear          // SES, ZCTA 2020, 2018-2022
capture confirm string variable ZCTA20
if _rc tostring ZCTA20, replace format(%05.0f)
save `ses2020'


# Our own data. `zip` is a label: say so, or pandas guesses "number" and
# 03042 becomes 3042.
mydata = pd.read_csv(DATA / "synthetic_data_v20260924.csv", dtype={"zip": str})

# NaNDA: Social Services, ZCTA 2010, 1990-2022. Same rule for the ZCTA code.
socialservices_zcta10 = pd.read_csv(
    DATA / "nanda" / "nanda_socials_Zcta10_1990-2022_01.csv", dtype={"zcta10": str}
)

# Parks and Socioeconomic Status: take the Stata format from ICPSR; pandas reads
# it without extra packages. Force every ZCTA code to five-character text.
def zcta_text(df, col):
    df[col] = df[col].astype(str).str.replace(r"\.0$", "", regex=True).str.zfill(5)
    return df

# The object keeps Robert's name, parks2022. The file is the 2018 ParkServe
# snapshot (DS0002, 2010 boundaries); ICPSR retitled it in October 2026.
parks2022_zcta10    = zcta_text(pd.read_stata(DATA / "nanda" / "38586-0002-Data.dta"), "ZCTA19")
ses2008_2017_zcta10 = zcta_text(pd.read_stata(DATA / "nanda" / "38528-0003-Data.dta"), "ZCTA10")
ses2018_2022_zcta20 = zcta_text(pd.read_stata(DATA / "nanda" / "38528-0008-Data.dta"), "ZCTA20")









WarningRead ZIP codes as text, always



ZIP codes are labels. Read them as numbers and 03042 becomes 3042 with no warning, and every join for that row fails. That is all of New England, New Jersey, and Puerto Rico dropping out of your analysis.

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
1. Which identifiers your data carry
Most survey and clinical datasets do not have geography. They have a string: an address, a city, a ZIP code, collected for mailing or billing, not for placing people in neighborhoods. That is the job now: to place each person in a neighborhood that another dataset has measured.
Before any merge, answer three questions about that string:

Which identifier do I have? An address, a ZIP code, a Census code?
How complete is it? Rows with nothing to look up never match.
What is it an identifier of? A ZIP code is a set of mail routes. An address becomes an identifier only after geocoding.

If your data already carry Census tract or ZCTA codes from an earlier geocoding step, those codes follow the boundaries of one census year, and the boundary question in Section 4 applies to them too.

What’s in the synthetic dataset








Variable
Type
Notes

2,004 unique; one row per person


year

2014–2025

zip missing for ~17% of rows

What NaNDA is published at
NaNDA describes neighborhoods, not people. Every measure is a count, a density, or a rate for a geographic unit in a given year. There are no individual records in the archive, so the linking is on you. NaNDA has no record of where your participants live.
Today we use three datasets from the NaNDA catalog on ICPSR:

NaNDA: Social Services (1990–2022)
NaNDA: Parks (2018, 2022)
NaNDA: Socioeconomic Status (2008–2022, two files)

All three are released at the Census tract level and the ZCTA level. We use the ZCTA files, because ZIP codes are what the synthetic data can offer. Every file we join to is drawn on 2010 boundaries. Robert Melendez explains that choice in the session, and Section 4 shows what changes when you mix boundary years.
Our file has ZIP codes and NaNDA has ZCTAs. They look alike, usually the same five digits, and they are not the same thing. Section 3 is about that gap.

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
2. If you have addresses: geocoding
A street address is the most precise location most studies collect, but it cannot be joined to anything until it is geocoded. Geocoding turns it into a point on the map. A spatial join then places that point inside a Census tract, and the tract-level NaNDA file joins on the tract code.
The route, step by step:

Geocode. Send each address to a geocoding service and get back coordinates plus a precision code. The Census Bureau’s geocoder is free and returns the tract directly. tidygeocoder in R talks to OpenStreetMap, ArcGIS, Google, and others through one interface.
Check precision. A rooftop match and a “somewhere in this city” match both come back with coordinates. Keep the tract only where the match is precise enough to trust. With OpenStreetMap, that is the place rank.
Spatial join to 2010 tracts. Download the TIGER/Line tract boundaries for the census year your NaNDA file uses and intersect the points with them.
Join to the tract-level NaNDA file on the tract code, then run the same diagnostics as Section 4.

Why we are not doing it live:

It is slow and it costs. Free services throttle to about one address per second. Paid ones charge per thousand addresses.
It is a terms-of-service question. Some services restrict storing or sharing the results, so a geocoded file may not be shareable even when the addresses are.
It fails differently. Addresses that will not parse, apartment-level ambiguity, and PO boxes all produce a coordinate or nothing, and the failure never looks like a join error.

The shape of it in R, using OpenStreetMap:
library(tidygeocoder)   # one interface to many geocoding services
library(tigris)         # Census boundary files
library(sf)             # spatial joins

mydata_geocoded <- mydata %>%
  geocode(street = address, city = city, state = state, postalcode = zip,
          method = "osm", full_results = TRUE)

# Keep a tract only where the match is precise enough (OSM place_rank >= 26).
points <- mydata_geocoded %>%
  filter(!is.na(lat)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)

tracts2010 <- tracts(state = unique(mydata$state), cb = FALSE, year = 2010)
points <- st_transform(points, st_crs(tracts2010))

mydata_tract10 <- st_join(points, tracts2010, join = st_intersects) %>%
  mutate(tract_fips10 = if_else(place_rank >= 26, GEOID10, NA_character_)) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()
From here the tract-level NaNDA files join on tract_fips10 exactly as the ZCTA files join on zcta10 below. Everything in Section 4 applies unchanged. The complete script is in your materials as r/geocode_to_tract.R, with a Python version beside it and a Stata version that goes through the Census Geocoder instead; each language folder’s README says what it needs and how long it takes.

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
3. ZIP is not ZCTA
A ZIP code is a Postal Service artifact. It names a set of delivery routes, and it was built for mail delivery.

Some ZIP codes are a single building.
Some are a bank of post office boxes with no residents.
Some cross county and state lines.
The Postal Service redraws them whenever the mail requires, without telling anyone doing research.

A ZCTA, a ZIP Code Tabulation Area, is the Census Bureau’s answer to the fact that researchers use ZIP codes anyway. For each decennial census, the Bureau assigns every census block to the ZIP code most of its addresses carry. The result is a set of areas with the same five-digit names as ZIP codes that tile the country and can be measured. NaNDA’s ZCTA files are built on these.
Most of the time a ZIP code and the ZCTA of the same name cover roughly the same people. ZIP codes with no ZCTA, such as post office boxes and single-site ZIPs, have nowhere to go. ZIPs mostly absorbed into a neighboring ZCTA are assigned there, under a different number. So the step from ZIP to ZCTA is a lookup against a crosswalk, not a rename of the column. And the crosswalk follows the boundaries of one census year, like everything else.

The crosswalk we’re using

UDS Mapper ZIP Code to ZCTA Crosswalk (2019 release, archived copy). Included in the ZIP as data/zip_to_zcta_2019.xlsx.
NaNDA’s published merge code: Chenoweth & Khan, code for merging NaNDA ZCTA-level datasets with the UDS Mapper crosswalk (2024).

Use the published merge code rather than a snippet copied from a screen. It is citable and maintained.

RStataPython



# Every column as text, for the same reason as `zip` above. Then pad back to five
# characters: whatever stripped a leading zero upstream did it before we got here.
zipzctaxwalk2019 <- read_excel(
  here("data", "zip_to_zcta_2019.xlsx"),
  col_types = "text"
) %>%
  mutate(
    ZIP_CODE = str_pad(ZIP_CODE, 5, pad = "0"),
    ZCTA     = str_pad(ZCTA,     5, pad = "0")
  )

# zip_join_type records how each ZIP was assigned its ZCTA, or that it has
# none. Check it before joining.

import numpy as np
mydata_zcta10.assign(zcta_status=np.select(
    [mydata_zcta10["zip"].isna(), mydata_zcta10["zcta10"].isna()],
    ["no ZIP", "ZIP not in crosswalk"], default="has a ZCTA",
))["zcta_status"].value_counts()









ImportantWhich ZCTA boundaries does your crosswalk produce?



The 2019 release of the UDS Mapper ZIP Code to ZCTA Crosswalk produces 2010-boundary ZCTAs. That makes it the right partner for NaNDA’s 2010-boundary files, which is what we use throughout. With your own data, read the crosswalk’s documentation for its target boundaries before anything else.




Who did you lose?
The table above gives the size of the loss. The diagnostic is whether the rows that did not get a ZCTA differ from the rows that did, and it belongs here, before anything from NaNDA is attached.
In this file about 17% of rows have no ZIP at all. If those rows are disproportionately rural, older, or in worse health, the matched sample is no longer the sample you drew. Every neighborhood coefficient you estimate is then conditional on having a mailable address. That is a selection problem, and no output flags it.
Neither language does this for you. Isolate the rows without a ZCTA and put their means beside the others’ means on the variables the study is about.

RStataPython



# Compare the rows that matched with those that did not, on the variables the
# study is about.
mydata_zcta10 %>%
  group_by(has_zcta = !is.na(zcta10)) %>%
  summarise(
    n                 = n(),
    loneliness        = round(mean(loneliness,        na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    physical_activity = round(mean(physical_activity, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    own_pet           = round(mean(own_pet,           na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
section: 4. Which boundaries? Joining, and checking the join
text:
4. Which boundaries? Joining, and checking the join
The join itself rarely goes wrong. If a column name is misspelled the software says so. The errors come from the inputs and from what you do with the result, and they are easy to miss.

Silent error 1: boundaries. ZCTA boundaries were redrawn for 2020. Most codes kept their five digits but changed their edges; some were added, dropped, or split. A 2010 code joined to a 2020 file usually finds a row, and the row usually describes approximately the same place. Your results will not show which matches were approximate.
Silent error 2: never looking at what fell out. A left join keeps every row of your data and fills NaNDA’s columns with NA where nothing matched. An inner join drops those rows. Either way the analysis proceeds. Stata’s merge reports _merge. R’s dplyr joins report nothing, so the count has to be built by hand.

The rest of this section is mostly diagnostics.

Carrying Social Services forward
Social Services ends in 2022; our data runs to 2025. Before joining, we give every ZCTA rows through 2025 and carry its most recent values into them. This is a modeling decision: the 2023 to 2025 rows will match, but they carry 2022’s numbers. State it in your methods.

RStataPython



# complete() adds the missing ZCTA-year rows; fill() carries each ZCTA's last
# value down into them. fill() does not stop at 2022: any value missing inside
# 1990-2022 (population, and the densities where population is zero) also gets
# the year before.
socialservices_zcta10 <- socialservices_zcta10 %>%
  complete(zcta10, year = 1990:2025) %>%

WarningMatch the boundaries, and say which ones you matched



Every code in a join follows the boundaries of one census year: the codes in your file, the codes the crosswalk produces, and the codes the NaNDA file is drawn on. All three have to agree. Ours agree on 2010. If your data run past 2019 and you want 2020 boundaries instead, use a crosswalk that produces 2020 codes and the 2020-boundary NaNDA files, and state the choice in your methods. Three reasons appear, and they call for different responses:

No ZIP is the big one and a data-collection problem. Nothing downstream fixes it.
ZIP not in the crosswalk is a typo or a ZIP newer than the crosswalk.
ZCTA not in the NaNDA file usually means the two were drawn on different boundaries.

At two rows apiece the last two vanish inside a match rate. In real data they point to a misalignment upstream, which is why the table lists reasons and not just a count. The fourth reason, year past coverage, is absent only because we carried Social Services forward. Without that step, 407 rows would sit in that line. Either way it is a limit of the NaNDA file, and a decision to document. If the reasons table shows anything beyond what Section 3 already explained, run the who-did-you-lose comparison again on in_nanda.

    mydata_nanda["count_totindivfamilyservices"],
    bins=[-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, np.inf],
    labels=["0", "1", "2", "3", "4-5", "6-10", "11+"],
)

# pandas has no models. statsmodels is the one extra package this step needs
# (pip install statsmodels); everything above runs without it.
try:
    import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
except ImportError:
    smf = None
    print("statsmodels is not installed; skipping the toy model.")

if smf is not None:
    own_pet_model = smf.logit(
        "own_pet ~ hot_meal_days + C(count_totindivfamilyservices_6cat) + C(ANY_OPEN_PARK) + AFFLUENCE",
        data=mydata_nanda.dropna(subset=["count_totindivfamilyservices_6cat", "ANY_OPEN_PARK", "AFFLUENCE"]),
    ).fit()
    print(own_pet_model.summary())









TipFour questions to ask before every link




What location information do my data contain? An address, a ZIP code, a Census code?
Which census year’s boundaries do my codes follow, and which does the NaNDA file follow?
Which crosswalk did I use, and which boundaries does it produce?
How many rows matched, and do the unmatched rows look different from the rest?

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
5. Now what?
Grace Noppert closes with a few minutes on why the link is worth making. Your data plus NaNDA data, joined on one geographic identifier, is a file that can answer questions neither could alone. The three measures we attached today each open one:

Social connection. Do older adults near more social services report less loneliness?
Physical activity. Is park access tied to staying active with age?
Food security. Does neighborhood disadvantage shape who goes without a hot meal?

Two cautions:

A neighborhood measure describes a place. Be clear when it is context and when it is a proxy for exposure.
People in the same ZCTA are not independent observations. The analysis has to account for that.

If one of these questions is close to yours, NaNDA has the measure and the catalog is where to start.
The materials ZIP holds:

the synthetic data and its codebook
the crosswalk
this notebook as a runnable notebook.qmd, and the same steps as standalone scripts in r/, stata/ and python/, under the same block headers. Each folder also has a tract version of the merge, for data that already carries a 2010 tract ID
an offline copy of this page

The NaNDA files are the one thing not in the ZIP. They come from ICPSR, which asks for a free account, so you download your own. It takes about five minutes, and data/nanda/README.md in the ZIP walks you through it. You only need them to re-run the code. If you use these materials in teaching or in a paper, cite them by the DOI below. It always resolves to the latest version.

Take this with you

If you do want to run along






NoteOptional setup (about 10 minutes, do it before the day)






R (4.3 or newer): cran.r-project.org
RStudio Desktop (free): posit.co
Open RStudio and run:
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "here", "janitor"))
(readxl, which reads the crosswalk, installs as part of tidyverse.)
Download and unzip the workshop materials.
Get the NaNDA files from ICPSR. Sign in at icpsr.umich.edu with a free account, then download these in R format (Stata and delimited versions are on the same pages):

NaNDA: Social Services: the ZCTA 2010 file.
NaNDA: Parks: dataset 2 (DS0002), “Parks by ZIP Code Tabulation Area, 2018 (2010 Boundaries)”.
NaNDA: Socioeconomic Status: datasets 3 and 8 (DS0003 and DS0008).

Unzip each one, extract the data file from the nested folders, and put all four in data/nanda/ inside the unzipped workshop folder. data/nanda/README.md has the filenames and the same steps in more detail.
Open workshop.Rproj, then open notebook.qmd, and run the first chunk. If it prints a preview of the data, you’re set.

Stata and Python users: equivalent .do files are in the stata/ folder of the ZIP and .py scripts in python/. The live session is in R, but these do the same thing step for step and are yours to keep. The R code is also there as plain scripts in r/, and each folder carries a second script for data that already has a 2010 tract ID instead of a ZIP code.

What we assume you already know
You have used R, Stata, or another statistical package to open a dataset and join two tables. This session covers what goes wrong when you link individual-level data to neighborhood-level data, and how to catch it, in whichever language you use.
